text: Room opened — goal: Deliver: Push link coverage toward 100% at +5%/day (the access gate)

name: Reel
text: We should prioritize adding more internal links between related content on our site. This decision improves our link coverage quickly by creating connections where they logically belong, helping users find relevant information while also boosting our search engine optimization. The trade-off is that this could divert our focus from larger, more time-consuming projects, but the immediate impact on link coverage makes it a strategic choice for our goal of reaching 100% coverage efficiently.

name: Scriv
text: I'm not convinced that just adding more internal links is the best approach, as it may lead to link clutter and dilute the value of our existing content. A better alternative might be to focus on creating high-quality, authoritative content that naturally attracts links from other reputable sources, which would not only improve link coverage but also enhance our site's credibility. To settle this, I'd like to see data on how internal linking has impacted our site's user engagement and search engine rankings in the past, to determine if it's really the most effective strategy.

name: Chisel
text:
**Decision: Run a "link audit sprint" to find and fix broken internal links first.**

This is the fastest way to push our link coverage up because broken links hurt our score more than missing ones. We’ll clean up the existing mess before adding new ones, which keeps users from hitting dead ends and tells search engines our site is well-maintained. The trade-off is that we’re not adding new links right away, but fixing broken ones is low-effort and high-impact—it’s like patching holes in a bucket before filling it.

name: Sift
text: While addressing broken links is undoubtedly important, focusing solely on this could delay our progress in improving overall link coverage. There's a real risk that we overlook the opportunity to create new, contextual internal links that enhance user experience and SEO simultaneously. A better approach might be to implement a parallel strategy: conduct the link audit while also establishing a plan for generating new links, ensuring we're not only fixing problems but also moving forward in our link-building efforts. Clear metrics on user engagement post-fixes could help settle this debate.

name: Scope
text:
**Decision: Run a "link audit sprint" to find and fix broken internal links first.**

This is the fastest way to push our link coverage up because broken links hurt our score more than missing ones. We’ll clean up the existing mess before adding new ones, which keeps users from hitting dead ends and avoids wasting effort on links that don’t even work. The trade-off is that we’ll delay adding fresh, high-value internal links in the short term—but fixing broken ones first ensures our foundation is solid before we build higher.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: I’m not convinced a "link audit sprint" alone is the fastest path to +5% daily coverage. The real risk is that we’ll burn days fixing what’s already broken while missing low-hanging fruit—like linking from high-traffic pages to related but orphaned content where users are already looking. A better alternative is to split the sprint: audit *and* add 2–3 strategic links per high-value page first, then circle back to fix what’s broken. That way, we prove coverage gains daily while still cleaning up the mess—no trade-off needed.

name: Echo
text: DECISION: Run a hybrid approach, combining a "link audit sprint" to fix broken internal links with a simultaneous effort to add new, contextual internal links from high-traffic pages to related content, delivered as a concrete plan with measurable link coverage improvements, owned by the team, with me, Echo, ensuring the record is complete and accurate.
